overview.title: Quick overview
overview.summary: Learn how an AI task becomes a search problem, how different representations guide a solution, and how to judge whether a method is useful.
outcomes: Identify the states, goals, actions, and costs in a problem.
Compare state-space search, problem reduction, and production rules.
Use completeness, cost, time, and memory to discuss a method.

blocks.text: Name the pieces

A search problem begins with a set of possible states, an initial state, and one or more goal states. Actions can move an agent from one state to another, while a transition model describes each change.
A path is a sequence of actions. A solution is a path that reaches a goal. An action cost can help compare possible paths when some solutions are more expensive than others.
Keep the useful details

A good abstraction leaves out details that do not affect the decision while preserving actions that still work in the real situation. Imagine a route from a library to a classroom: locations are states, walking is an action, and reaching the classroom is the goal.
Choose a useful formulation
A standardized task has a precise setup that makes methods easy to compare. A real-world task usually brings extra constraints, incomplete information, and choices that depend on context.

Ask whether a large task can be divided into smaller tasks. Also ask what happens after an action: can it be ignored, undone, or is it irreversible? These properties affect which search method is suitable.
Knowledge and uncertainty

An AI method may need a substantial knowledge base, human input, and a way to handle uncertain or irrelevant information. Heuristics guide search when exhaustive exploration is impractical; learning can improve behavior from experience.
Forward and backward search

State-space search treats each possible situation as a state and actions as connections. Forward search starts at the initial state and explores actions toward a goal. Backward search starts from a goal description and asks which earlier actions could lead to it.
Make a state concrete
In a sliding-tile puzzle, a state records where the tiles are. In a water-jug task, a pair of numbers can record the amount in each jug. Moves or pours create the next state.
Know the limit
A state space can become too large to list or explore completely. Time and memory limits matter, so a useful representation and a selective search strategy are important.
Break it into subproblems
Problem reduction replaces one difficult task with smaller tasks whose results can be combined. The structure can be described with AND and OR relationships.
With AND, every required subproblem must be solved. With OR, solving any one of several alternatives is enough.
Try an everyday example
A class trip may need both transport and permission forms: that is an AND relationship. If transport can be a bus or a train, choosing either acceptable option is an OR relationship.
Use condition and action rules
A production rule pairs an IF condition with a THEN action. Working memory holds the current facts. When a condition matches those facts, the rule can be applied and working memory may change.
A control system chooses which applicable rule to use and when to stop. A rule applier carries out that choice. When several rules match, the system needs a conflict-resolution strategy.
Choose among matching rules
A system might prefer a more specific rule, a rule based on recent facts, or the first rule in an ordered list. Refraction prevents a fired rule from repeating until its matching facts change.
Rules are modular and can be edited independently. As a rule set grows, however, overlapping rules and hard-to-follow control flow require careful review.
Ask four performance questions

Completeness asks whether a method can find a solution when one exists. Cost optimality asks whether it can find a least-cost solution. Time complexity concerns the work needed; space complexity concerns memory.
Describe search size
Branching factor is the number of next states a step may create. Solution depth counts the actions in an optimal path, while maximum path length describes how long any explored path could become.
These measures help compare methods for the same problem. A method that works well for a small state space may become too slow or memory-hungry for a larger one.
